name: The '80s
blurb: Synths, big hair and MTV: the decade when music learned to look as good as it sounded.

questions.prompt: Which song was the first music video shown on MTV when it launched on August 1, 1981?
questions.fact: The Buggles recorded the song in 1979, and MTV picked it as a wry statement of purpose for its debut.

questions.prompt: Who produced Michael Jackson's 1982 album Thriller?
questions.fact: Jones and Jackson had already worked together on Jackson's 1979 breakthrough, Off the Wall.

questions.prompt: Which Minneapolis musician starred in the 1984 film Purple Rain?
questions.fact: The film cost a few million dollars to make and grossed roughly ten times its budget.

questions.prompt: Live Aid was held on July 13, 1985, at stadiums in which two cities?
questions.fact: Bob Geldof organized it after the Band Aid single, which he co-wrote with Midge Ure of Ultravox.

questions.prompt: Which singer had a 1983 hit with "Girls Just Want to Have Fun"?
questions.fact: Robert Hazard wrote and demoed the song, and Lauper changed the words to give it a female point of view.

questions.prompt: Which band recorded "Don't Stop Believin'" for its 1981 album Escape?
questions.fact: Keyboardist Jonathan Cain has said the title came from his father, who urged him not to give up when he moved to California.

questions.prompt: Which duo had a 1984 hit with "Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go"?
questions.fact: The title reportedly came from a note Andrew Ridgeley left for his parents, in which he accidentally wrote the word "up" twice.

questions.prompt: Which band named its 1987 album after a tree that grows in the California desert?
questions.fact: Photographer Anton Corbijn shot the sleeve in the California desert, and the album was produced by Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois.

questions.prompt: Which New Jersey rocker released the 1984 album Born in the U.S.A.?
questions.fact: The title song is about a Vietnam veteran's hard homecoming, and it was often misread as a flag-waving anthem.

questions.prompt: What was the title of Tina Turner's 1984 comeback album?
questions.fact: Turner was 44 and had spent years rebuilding her career after leaving Ike Turner in 1976.

questions.prompt: Slash's famous opening riff on "Sweet Child o' Mine" began as what?
choices: A cover of an old blues tune
A finger exercise played as a joke
A bass part Duff McKagan wrote
A leftover riff from an earlier demo
questions.fact: Axl Rose wrote the words about his girlfriend Erin Everly, the daughter of Don Everly of the Everly Brothers.

questions.prompt: On which 1983 TV special did Michael Jackson first perform the moonwalk in front of a national audience?
questions.fact: Jackson performed "Billie Jean" at the show, and the moonwalk made the performance a landmark.

questions.prompt: In the 1989 film Say Anything..., John Cusack holds a boombox playing which Peter Gabriel song?
questions.fact: Cameron Crowe directed the film, and the scene became one of the most copied romantic gestures in movies.

questions.prompt: Which singer co-wrote 1985's "We Are the World" with Michael Jackson?
questions.fact: The stars recorded it in one night after the American Music Awards, with a sign on the studio door asking them to check their egos.

questions.prompt: In the video for a-ha's "Take On Me", a young woman is pulled into what?
questions.fact: The video, directed by Steve Barron, combined live action with pencil-sketch animation made by rotoscoping, and it took months of hand drawing.

questions.prompt: What studio effect gave Phil Collins's drums their huge sound on "In the Air Tonight"?
questions.fact: Engineer Hugh Padgham and Collins stumbled on the effect while recording a Peter Gabriel album, and it came to define the decade's drum sound.

questions.prompt: Which device did Richie Sambora use to make his guitar "talk" on "Livin' on a Prayer"?
questions.fact: The song was written by Jon Bon Jovi, Sambora and Desmond Child for the album Slippery When Wet.

questions.prompt: Tracy Chapman's career took off after a 1988 appearance at which concert?
choices: Amnesty International's Human Rights Now! tour
questions.fact: She went back on stage when Stevie Wonder's set was delayed, and her self-titled debut then soared up the charts.

questions.prompt: Which Police singer sings the "I want my MTV" lines on Dire Straits' "Money for Nothing"?
questions.fact: Sting received a songwriting credit because the line echoed the melody of "Don't Stand So Close to Me".

questions.prompt: Johnny Marr has said he turned up at the door of which singer in 1982 to suggest writing songs together?
questions.fact: The two went on to form the Smiths in Manchester.

questions.prompt: Huey Lewis said Ray Parker Jr.'s "Ghostbusters" resembled which of his own songs?
questions.fact: The two sides settled out of court, and the dispute later flared up again over a confidentiality agreement.

questions.prompt: Who wrote "Don't You (Forget About Me)", the song Simple Minds recorded for The Breakfast Club?
questions.fact: Billy Idol and Bryan Ferry reportedly turned the song down, and Simple Minds also hesitated before recording it.

questions.prompt: The title track of Prince's Purple Rain was recorded live at which Minneapolis venue?
questions.fact: Prince played the 1983 benefit show there with the Revolution, and the club also appears in the film.

questions.prompt: Who wrote Madonna's 1984 hit "Like a Virgin"?
questions.fact: The same pair also wrote Cyndi Lauper's "True Colors".

questions.prompt: Which British animation studio created the stop-motion effects for Peter Gabriel's "Sledgehammer" video?
questions.fact: Gabriel spent many hours lying under a sheet of glass for the shoot.

questions.prompt: Who wrote "Nothing Compares 2 U", which Sinead O'Connor made famous in 1990?
questions.fact: Prince wrote it in 1985 for the Family, a side project, and O'Connor's version became the best-known recording.

questions.prompt: Which Italian producer co-wrote Berlin's "Take My Breath Away" for the film Top Gun?
questions.fact: The song won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.

questions.prompt: Which South African group sang on Paul Simon's 1986 album Graceland?
questions.fact: Simon recorded in Johannesburg despite a cultural boycott of South Africa, which made the album controversial.

questions.prompt: A 2010 court ruling found the flute riff in Men at Work's "Down Under" borrowed from which song?
choices: Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree
questions.fact: The similarity became widely known after it was pointed out on an Australian television quiz show.

questions.prompt: Which singer was Whitney Houston's cousin?
questions.fact: Houston's mother, Cissy Houston, was a gospel singer, and Aretha Franklin was her godmother.

stories.title: I Want My MTV
stories.dek: The channel that changed how pop looked
stories.body:
At one minute past midnight on August 1, 1981, a new cable channel went on the air with a shot of the Apollo moon landing and a countdown. The first video it played was "Video Killed the Radio Star" by the Buggles. The channel was called MTV, short for Music Television, and its creators, including executive Bob Pittman, thought young viewers might want to watch songs the way they listened to the radio.

The beginning was modest. MTV reached only a few cable systems at first, and in New York and Los Angeles viewers could not get it at all. The channel had little to play, because few artists had made videos. Many of the early clips came from Britain, where bands had been filming promotional shorts for years since there were few television shows to appear on. That helped acts like Duran Duran, Adam Ant and Culture Club, who looked as good on screen as they sounded.

Then came a clever campaign. Cable operators were asked to carry the channel, and viewers were urged to phone their local systems and demand it. Mick Jagger and other stars appeared in ads saying the line that gave the channel its slogan, "I want my MTV." It worked, and by the mid-1980s the channel was in tens of millions of homes.

Soon a video could make a hit. Michael Jackson's "Billie Jean" and "Thriller" were treated as events, and MTV's rotation helped him reach a huge audience. Some accounts say CBS Records pressed the channel to play his work, because it had played few Black artists in its early days. Details of that story vary, but Jackson's videos did break the barrier. Madonna, Prince and Peter Gabriel followed, along with a-ha, whose pencil-sketch video for "Take On Me" drew viewers who had never heard the song.

The change was lasting. Artists now thought about how a song would look as well as how it sounded, and directors became part of the music business. Some older fans grumbled that the pictures got in the way of the music. But for a generation, the decade's songs came with images attached, and those images are still how many people remember them.

stories.title: Live Aid
stories.dek: Sixteen hours, two stadiums and a billion viewers
stories.body:
In October 1984, Irish singer Bob Geldof was watching the BBC news when he saw a report from Ethiopia by Michael Buerk. It showed thousands of people suffering from a famine. Geldof, the leader of the Boomtown Rats, felt he had to act. He called Midge Ure of Ultravox, and together they wrote a Christmas song, "Do They Know It's Christmas?" Dozens of British stars, calling themselves Band Aid, recorded it in a single day in November 1984. It became the best-selling single in British history at the time.

Geldof was not finished. He wanted a concert, and he wanted it to be enormous. On July 13, 1985, Live Aid took place at Wembley Stadium in London and John F. Kennedy Stadium in Philadelphia, with the shows overlapping and broadcast around the world. Organizers estimated a television audience of well over a billion people in around 150 countries, though such numbers are only estimates.

The lineup was remarkable. In London, Status Quo opened with "Rockin' All Over the World," and later acts included U2, Elton John, David Bowie and Paul McCartney. Queen's set is often called one of the great live performances in rock, with Freddie Mercury leading the Wembley crowd in a call-and-response. In Philadelphia the acts included Bob Dylan, Tina Turner, Madonna, and a reunited Led Zeppelin.

Phil Collins played in both cities. After performing at Wembley he flew across the Atlantic on the supersonic Concorde and then played in Philadelphia, first with his own songs and then on drums for Led Zeppelin. It was a stunt that fit the day's spirit of excess.

The concert raised a large sum for famine relief, and money kept arriving afterward. Critics later argued about how the funds were spent and whether charity concerts were the right approach. But no one doubted the effect. For one day, the music world had come together for a single cause, and the template of the benefit concert was set for decades.

Geldof received an honorary knighthood in 1986 for his work.

stories.title: Purple Rain
stories.dek: A club in Minneapolis and a song once meant for Stevie Nicks
stories.body:
Prince Rogers Nelson grew up in Minneapolis, a cold Midwestern city that was not an obvious home for a pop revolution. By 1983 he had already recorded several albums, and he was ready to make a film and a record that would make him a star. He gathered a band called the Revolution, which included guitarist Wendy Melvoin and keyboardist Lisa Coleman, and built his new project around them.

On August 3, 1983, he played a benefit concert at First Avenue, the Minneapolis nightclub where he had performed since his early days. The show was recorded. Three songs from that night, including the long, anthemic title track "Purple Rain," made the album, with some studio touch-ups added later. Hearing the final version, it is easy to picture the sweat and noise in the room.

The song has an odd backstory. Prince first thought of it as a country-flavored ballad, and he reportedly asked Stevie Nicks of Fleetwood Mac to write words for it. She listened to the long instrumental track and felt overwhelmed, and she said she could not do it. Prince went back and finished the song himself. It turned into a slow, rising rock ballad with a long guitar solo at the end.

The film, directed by Albert Magnoli, came out in July 1984. Prince played a talented but troubled young musician called the Kid, and the story drew loosely on his own life. It cost a few million dollars and earned many times that. The album became one of the best-selling of the decade, with hits like "When Doves Cry" and "Let's Go Crazy". It also won Prince an Academy Award for Best Original Song Score.

The record changed what a pop star could be. Prince wrote, produced and played nearly everything himself on many tracks, yet he gave his band a visible place on stage. He went on to make a string of striking albums through the rest of the decade.

First Avenue became a landmark, and its black exterior is now covered with stars honoring the performers who have played there.

stories.title: U2 at Red Rocks
stories.dek: Rain, mist and a white flag in Colorado, June 1983.
stories.body:
In June 1983 U2 were a young Irish band with a growing following, and they had just released their third album, War. They were not yet stars in the United States. On June 5 they played the Red Rocks Amphitheatre outside Denver, a spectacular outdoor venue carved between two giant slabs of red sandstone. It was a show that was supposed to be filmed for television and video.

The weather did not cooperate. Rain fell during the afternoon and into the evening, and a heavy mist hung over the stage. At first it seemed to threaten the whole shoot. As the show began, however, the fog and low clouds began to look dramatic on film, and the band, soaked and determined, delivered a charged performance.

Some of the most striking images came during Sunday Bloody Sunday, when Bono carried a white flag onto the stage and later climbed the rocks and scaffolding while singing. The song was about the violence in Northern Ireland, and the flag was a symbol of peace and surrender to hatred. Torches burned in the background, and the band's guitarist, the Edge, played jangling, echoing chords that bounced off the stone walls. The set also included New Year's Day, Gloria and I Will Follow.

The performance was released as a concert film, U2 Live at Red Rocks: Under a Blood Red Sky, and parts of the show were included on a live album with the same name later in 1983. The album was recorded at several places, but the video from Red Rocks gave fans an image of the band that they would remember. It was shown on MTV, which had only recently begun to feature rock bands regularly, and it made U2 look larger than life.

The film is widely credited with helping the band's career in the United States. It showed that U2 could hold a huge audience with songs and a visual style that was entirely their own. In the following years the band would build on that foundation with The Unforgettable Fire and then The Joshua Tree, which included With or Without You.

The story is a good example of luck turning into legend. A rainy night that looked like a disaster ended up as one of the defining concerts of the decade.

stories.title: Mandela at Wembley
stories.dek: A tribute concert in June 1988 and a quiet singer who stole it.
stories.body:
On June 11, 1988, a crowd of about 72,000 gathered at Wembley Stadium in London for a concert to mark Nelson Mandela's seventieth birthday. Mandela was still in prison in South Africa, where he had been held for decades, and the event was meant to focus attention on the struggle against apartheid. The show was broadcast in many countries, and organizers reported that hundreds of millions of people watched.

The lineup included Dire Straits, Whitney Houston, Stevie Wonder, Sting, Peter Gabriel, Eurythmics and many others, along with comedians and actors who spoke between songs. Because the tribute was so large, the schedule was packed, and the performers each had a few minutes to make their mark.

Among them was a young singer and guitarist named Tracy Chapman. She had released her first album only a few months earlier, and she was little known beyond a few clubs and campuses. Chapman came on early in the day, with only her acoustic guitar, and sang Talkin' Bout a Revolution to a crowd that was still finding its seats. Her calm voice and plain approach stood out.

Later in the evening, Stevie Wonder ran into trouble with his equipment, and the program had to be delayed. The organizers needed someone who could step in with little preparation. Chapman, who had not planned to play again, was reportedly asked to come back, and she did. She sang Fast Car alone on stage, in front of the full crowd and a worldwide television audience. The performance was quiet and direct, and many viewers saw in it something they had not heard in the arena rock around her.

In the weeks that followed, interest in her debut album grew sharply. Fast Car, which tells the story of a couple trying to escape poverty, found a huge audience on the radio. Chapman went on to win several Grammy Awards at the beginning of 1989, including Best New Artist.

The concert had a political effect, too. It brought the issue of apartheid to a vast audience, and it increased pressure on the South African government. Mandela was released from prison in 1990, and four years later he became the country's president.

For Chapman, Wembley turned a debut into a breakthrough. She did it with a guitar, a voice and a song that did not need anything else.

covers.title: Tainted Love
covers.note: Ed Cobb wrote it, and Gloria Jones, who later became Marc Bolan's partner, released it in 1964. Soft Cell's synth version reached number one in the UK.

covers.title: I Love Rock 'n' Roll
covers.note: Alan Merrill and Jake Hooker wrote it, and Merrill's band the Arrows recorded it in 1975. Jett reportedly heard the Arrows play it on British TV while on tour.

covers.title: Venus
covers.note: The Dutch band Shocking Blue took it to number one in the US in 1970. Bananarama's 1986 version, produced by Stock Aitken Waterman, also reached number one in the US.

covers.title: Pass the Dutchie
covers.note: The Mighty Diamonds recorded it as Pass the Kouchie. Musical Youth, a group of British schoolboys, reportedly changed the word to dutchie, the Jamaican word for a cooking pot.

covers.title: Funky Town
covers.note: Steven Greenberg wrote and produced it as Lipps Inc., with Cynthia Johnson singing. It appeared on the 1979 album Mouth to Mouth and went to number one in the US in 1980. The Australian band Pseudo Echo took it into the US top ten in 1987.

covers.title: Dancing in the Street
covers.note: Marvin Gaye co-wrote it, and Martha and the Vandellas had the 1964 hit. Bowie and Jagger recorded it for Live Aid famine relief, and it went to number one in the UK.

covers.title: You Keep Me Hangin' On
covers.note: Holland-Dozier-Holland wrote it for the Supremes' 1966 number one. Wilde's electropop version also reached number one in the US.

covers.title: Red Red Wine
covers.note: Diamond wrote it for his 1967 album Just for You. UB40's reggae version, reportedly based on Tony Tribe's 1969 cover, reached number one in the UK in 1983 and in the US in 1988.
